intro: Who gets to stand on the mat is decided by rules, laws and governments, not only by coaches. A weight sheet can leave out every woman. A school order can require every boy to take kendo. An army of occupation can close a practice hall. In this unit you will read those rules and the reasons written beside them.

The first chapter follows women and girls into judo, wrestling, taekwondo, fencing and sumo. You will meet a federal law, a medal taken back and a rank limit that lasted decades. The second chapter follows governments in Japan, the Soviet Union and China as they put combat arts into schools and national programs.

By the end, you will be able to explain how a law or an order changed who could compete. You will also compare the reasons governments gave with what else they were doing at the time, using dates as evidence.
bigQuestion: Who decides who may stand on the mat, and what reasons do they give?

title: Who May Stand on the Mat

chapters.title: Women on the Mat
chapters.bigQuestion: Why did women and girls reach the mat, the ring and the Olympic program later than men, and who opened those doors?

story.title: The New Weight Sheet
story.kicker: One printed page shows who a sport expects to see.
paragraphs: A wrestling official tapes a sheet to the wall beside the scale. It lists weight classes, one per line, with a blank for each wrestler's name. Older sheets from the same sport had only one column of classes. Every name on them belonged to a man or a boy.

This sheet has a second column. Its heading reads women. The classes in it are set at different weights, and the names are new. Some of the wrestlers on it started on boys' teams because no girls' team existed in their school.

A weight sheet looks like paperwork. Yet it decides who may compete, against whom, and for which title. When a governing body adds a column, it admits that a group of athletes belongs in its official records. Before that, those athletes could train but could not win the sport's own championships.

In combat sports, that change came slowly. Women's fencing reached the Olympics in 1924. Women's judo waited until 1992, wrestling until 2004 and boxing until 2012. Each new column followed years of work by athletes, coaches and lawmakers whose names are part of the record.
story.think: What can a weight sheet tell a historian about who a sport included in a given year?

lessons.title: Title IX in 1972
lessons.mainIdea: Title IX, passed in 1972, banned sex discrimination in schools and colleges that receive federal money.
reading: On June 23, 1972, President Richard Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972. One short part of that law is called *Title IX*. It says no person may be shut out of a school program because of sex. The rule covers any school or college that takes federal money.

Title IX did not name sports at all. Its authors were thinking about admissions, jobs and classes. Representative Patsy Mink of Hawaii was one of its main authors. After her death in 2002, Congress renamed the law the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act.

Schools soon learned that sports counted as an education program. Girls' teams, budgets and coaches began to grow in high schools and colleges. The law became the main tool for *equal opportunity* in American school sport.

words.d: the part of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bans sex discrimination in education programs receiving federal money
a fair chance to take part, without being shut out because of who you are
belonging to the national government of the United States

look.title: The Words of Title IX
look.text: No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
look.cite: Title IX, Education Amendments of 1972, Section 901(a)
look.prompt: The law never uses the word sport. Which words in it made schools apply it to teams?

check.q: Why did Title IX come to cover school sports?

lessons.title: The Contact Sport Exception
lessons.mainIdea: Rules written in 1975 let schools keep separate teams in contact sports, so wrestling and boxing changed slowly.
reading: Title IX needed detailed rules to be enforced. The federal government issued them in 1975. One rule said a school could run separate teams for boys and girls. It also named certain sports as *contact sports*.

The list of contact sports included boxing, wrestling, rugby, ice hockey, football and basketball. In a contact sport, a school did not have to let a girl try out for the boys' team. It also did not have to start a girls' team if few girls asked for one.

This *exception* shaped combat sports for decades. Many schools added girls' basketball, which was on the list, because many girls wanted to play. Girls' wrestling grew far later. For years, a girl who wanted to wrestle often had to ask to join the boys' team.

words.d: a sport in which athletes are expected to touch or collide; the 1975 Title IX rules named several
a case a rule leaves out on purpose
a detailed rule a government agency writes to carry out a law

lessons.title: Girls Build Their Own Teams
lessons.mainIdea: Girls' wrestling grew state by state, and college women's wrestling gained NCAA recognition in 2020.
reading: Through the 1980s and 1990s, some American girls wrestled on boys' high school teams. They trained and competed under the boys' *weight classes*. A few won matches at state tournaments. Their results showed coaches that girls wanted the sport.

Some states then created separate girls' championships. Illinois held its first IHSA girls' state finals in the 2021–22 season. Colleges moved too. Several small colleges started women's wrestling teams in the 1990s and 2000s.

In 2020 the NCAA named women's wrestling an *emerging sport*. That label means the NCAA helps colleges add a women's sport that is still growing. It moves a sport toward an official NCAA championship. Girls' and women's wrestling is now one of the fastest growing school sports.

words.d: a group of athletes of about the same body weight who compete against each other
an NCAA label for a growing women's sport that colleges are encouraged to add

lessons.title: A Medal Taken Back
lessons.mainIdea: In 1959 Rusty Kanokogi won a judo medal at a YMCA tournament in New York and was made to give it back because she was a woman.
reading: Rena Glickman grew up in Brooklyn, New York, and began judo in the 1950s. People called her *Rusty*. In 1959 she entered a YMCA judo tournament in upstate New York. She wore her hair short, and her team entered her in the men's contest.

Her team won. Then officials learned she was a woman and asked for her medal back. They said the rules did not allow women in the contest. She gave it back, but she did not leave judo. She later trained at the Kodokan in Tokyo and married Ryohei Kanokogi, a judo teacher.

The YMCA's choice shows how a *tournament rule* could close a sport without saying women could not train. Women were welcome in some judo clubs. What they lacked were official contests and titles. In 2008 the YMCA gave Kanokogi a new medal, almost fifty years later.

words.d: a rule a contest's organizers write about who may enter and how winners are named

lessons.title: A World Title for Women
lessons.mainIdea: In 1980 Kanokogi organized the first women's world judo championships, held at Madison Square Garden in New York.
reading: By the 1970s women's judo contests were growing in Europe, Japan and the Americas. Yet there was no women's *world championship*. Men's world judo championships had been held since 1956. Kanokogi decided to organize a women's one herself.

She raised money, found sponsors and even took out a loan on her home. In November 1980 the first women's world judo championships were held at Madison Square Garden in New York City. Athletes came from many countries. Official medals now existed for women at the world level.

Kanokogi then pressed the International Judo Federation and the International Olympic Committee to add women. Women's judo appeared as a *demonstration event* at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. It became a full medal sport four years later.

lessons.title: A Ceiling on Rank
lessons.mainIdea: For decades Kodokan women stopped at fifth dan; Keiko Fukuda was promoted to sixth dan in 1972 and ninth dan in 2006.
reading: A *dan* is a black-belt rank in judo. Higher numbers mark longer service and greater standing. For decades, women at the Kodokan did not rise above fifth dan. Men with similar years of teaching could go higher.

Keiko Fukuda moved to the United States and taught women's judo in San Francisco from the 1960s. Students and supporters argued that the rank limit was unfair. In 1972 the Kodokan promoted Fukuda to sixth dan. She was the first woman to pass the old limit.

In 2006 the Kodokan made her a ninth dan, the first woman to reach it there. In 2011 USA Judo awarded her tenth dan, its highest rank. She died in 2013. A *rank ceiling* is a quiet kind of exclusion, because it lets people in but stops how far they rise.

words.d: a black-belt rank in judo and other Japanese arts, counted upward from first
a limit on how high a group of people may be promoted
being moved up to a higher rank

check.why: A dan is a black-belt rank, counted upward from first.

check.q: Why is a rank ceiling a form of exclusion?

check.why: A rank ceiling admits people but stops their promotion at a set level.

lessons.title: Barcelona Adds Seven Classes
lessons.mainIdea: When women's judo became a medal sport in 1992, it arrived with seven weight classes, the same number as the men's.
reading: At the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, women's judo held seven *medal events*. The men also had seven. Each event is one weight class with its own gold, silver and bronze medals. Women's judo entered the Games at full size, not as a single trial event.

That choice was not true of every combat sport. Women's wrestling began in 2004 with four classes, while men had more. Women's boxing began in 2012 with only three, against ten for men. The number of classes decides how many women can win medals.

The *Olympic program* is the list of sports and events at one Games. The International Olympic Committee approves it after hearing from each federation. Adding a women's event often meant cutting or reshaping a men's event, because the total number of athletes is capped.

words.d: one contest at the Olympics that awards its own gold, silver and bronze
the list of sports and events held at one Olympic Games

lessons.title: Taekwondo Starts Even
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo entered the Olympics in 2000 with four weight classes for women and four for men.
reading: Taekwondo became a full Olympic medal sport at the Sydney Games in 2000. Unlike judo and wrestling, it had women's events from its first medal year. There were four weight classes for women and four for men.

The world body, now called World Taekwondo, had held women's world championships since 1987. So by 2000 there was already a pool of women with international records. The first women's Olympic taekwondo gold medal went to Lauren Burns of Australia, in the lightest class.

Olympic taekwondo has fewer classes than its world championships. Each Olympic class covers a wider *weight range*. That squeeze lets the sport fit inside the Olympic cap while keeping men's and women's events equal in number.

words.d: the span from the lightest to the heaviest body weight allowed in one class
the international federation that runs Olympic-style taekwondo

lessons.title: Wrestling Waits for Athens
lessons.mainIdea: Women's freestyle wrestling held world championships from 1987 but joined the Olympics only in 2004.
reading: Wrestling was part of the first modern Olympics in 1896. For more than a hundred years, only men wrestled there. Women's wrestling clubs grew in France, Norway, Japan and elsewhere in the 1970s and 1980s.

The world wrestling body held its first women's world championships in 1987, in Norway. The women wrestled *freestyle*, one of the two Olympic styles. Japan, China, the United States and Canada soon built strong women's programs.

Women's freestyle wrestling joined the Olympics at Athens in 2004 with four classes. In 2016 the program changed to six classes for women and six for each men's style. The *gap* between a first world title and a first Olympic medal was seventeen years.

words.d: one of the two Olympic wrestling styles, and the only one women compete in at the Games
the time between two events in a timeline

lessons.title: The Sumo Ring and a Medical Emergency
lessons.mainIdea: Professional sumo keeps women off its ring, and a 2018 emergency in Maizuru made that rule a national debate in Japan.
reading: The *dohyō* is the raised clay ring of sumo. The Japan Sumo Association, which runs professional sumo, does not let women step onto it. The association links the rule to tradition and to the ring's role in Shinto ceremonies. Critics in Japan call it sex discrimination.

On April 4, 2018, the mayor of Maizuru collapsed while giving a speech on a dohyō during a touring event. Several women from the crowd, including a nurse, climbed up to give him first aid. A referee announced over the speakers that women should leave the ring.

The association's chairman apologized and said life-saving care came first. Earlier, Osaka's governor, Fusae Ohta, had asked in 2000 to present a trophy on the ring herself and was refused. Meanwhile, amateur women's sumo holds its own contests and world championships.

words.d: the raised clay ring where sumo matches are held
the body that runs professional sumo in Japan
for athletes who are not paid to compete

lessons.title: Fencing One Weapon at a Time
lessons.mainIdea: Women's Olympic fencing began with foil in 1924, but épée waited until 1996 and sabre until 2004.
reading: Modern fencing uses three weapons: foil, épée and sabre. Each has its own rules about where a touch counts. Men fenced all three at the Olympics from the early 1900s. Women's fencing began with *foil* at the Paris Games of 1924.

For seventy years, foil was the only weapon women fenced at the Olympics. Many officials of the time judged it the proper weapon for women. Women's *épée* joined at Atlanta in 1996. Women's *sabre* joined at Athens in 2004.

Fencing shows that a sport can admit women early and still limit them. The first door opened in 1924. The last one opened eighty years later. Today women fence all three weapons, in both individual and team events.

chapters.title: When the State Uses the Gym
chapters.bigQuestion: When a government puts a martial art into its schools, is it building healthy people or serving its own plans?

story.title: A Memo About Gym Hours
story.kicker: A government order can turn a club art into a school subject.
paragraphs: A school principal in Japan opens an order from the Ministry of Education in the early 1930s. It concerns boys' middle schools. From now on, kendo or judo is a required part of physical education. The principal must find a teacher, a hall and hours in a crowded week.

The order gives reasons. Budo, it says, trains the body and builds strong character. The principal also knows the wider mood. Japan's army is fighting in Manchuria, and newspapers praise loyalty and discipline. A class in the gym now carries a message about the nation.

Fifteen years later, a very different order arrives. Japan has lost World War II. Under the Allied occupation, the ministry tells schools to stop teaching budo. Swords, jackets and wooden practice weapons are put away. The same hall that held a required class now stands empty of it.

Governments in many countries have used gyms this way. They have added arts to schools, taken them out and brought them back. Each time, the reasons written in the memo tell historians what the state wanted from its young people.
story.think: What can a school timetable reveal about what a government hopes students will become?

lessons.title: A National Hall in Kyoto
lessons.mainIdea: The Dai Nippon Butokukai, founded in Kyoto in 1895, joined many martial arts under one national body tied to the state.
reading: In 1895 Japan won a war against Qing China. That same year, leaders in Kyoto founded the *Dai Nippon Butokukai*, the Greater Japan Martial Virtue Society. Its founding matched the 1,100th anniversary of Kyoto becoming the capital. Members of the imperial family served as its honorary heads.

In 1899 the society opened the *Butokuden*, a large practice hall beside the Heian Shrine in Kyoto. It held yearly national demonstrations of kendo, judo, archery and other arts. Teachers came from every part of the country. The building still stands and is still used for martial arts.

The Butokukai gave teaching titles to senior teachers and ran a school that trained instructors. Its branches spread to every prefecture and to Japan's colonies. By joining many old schools under one roof, it made the martial arts look like a single national tradition.

words.d: the Greater Japan Martial Virtue Society, a national martial arts body founded in Kyoto in 1895
the Butokukai's great practice hall in Kyoto, opened in 1899
one of the regions Japan is divided into for government

lessons.title: From Choice to Requirement
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese middle schools could teach kendo and judo from 1911, and the government made one of them required for boys in 1931.
reading: Japan's public school system copied European models in the 1870s. Physical education meant marching and gymnastics. Supporters of kendo and judo, including Kanō Jigorō, argued for years that these arts should be taught in schools too.

In 1911 the Ministry of Education allowed middle schools to teach *gekiken*, the older word for kendo, and jujutsu as part of physical education. It was a choice, not a rule. Schools needed trained teachers, and the Butokukai's school helped supply them.

In 1931 the ministry made kendo or judo *compulsory* for boys in middle schools. That same year, Japan's army seized Manchuria in northeast China. Schools now described budo as training in loyalty and spirit, not only fitness. The gym had become part of the nation's plans.

words.d: an older Japanese name for sword fencing with bamboo swords, later called kendo
required by a rule; students must take it
the set of subjects a school must teach

lessons.title: Budo in Wartime
lessons.mainIdea: During World War II Japan's government took direct control of the Butokukai and used budo to prepare students for war.
reading: Official language changed in the 1910s and 1920s. The Butokukai began using *budo*, meaning martial ways, in place of bujutsu, meaning martial techniques. Gekiken became kendo. The new words stressed character and the path of a life.

After the war with China widened in 1937, schools gave more hours to budo. In 1942 the government reorganized the Butokukai as an official body. Several ministries, including the army and navy ministries, now helped run it. Schools taught budo as part of training students for war.

Many teachers and students experienced that time differently. Some saw the arts as sport and character building. Others served in the war. Historians use the wartime records to study how a state can shape a practice for its own goals, a process called *mobilization*.

words.d: martial ways; the name Japanese arts such as judo and kendo took in the early 1900s
a government gathering people and resources for war or another national goal

look.text: Students are told to honor their parents, be loyal and study. They are also told that, should an emergency arise, they should offer themselves bravely to the state.

check.why: In 1942 the government reorganized the Butokukai under several ministries.

check.q: What is mobilization?
choices: Gathering people and resources for a national goal
check.why: Mobilization means a government gathering people and resources, often for war.

lessons.title: The Occupation Stops Budo
lessons.mainIdea: After 1945 the Allied occupation removed budo from Japan's schools and dissolved the Butokukai in 1946.
reading: Japan surrendered in August 1945. The Allied occupation, led by U.S. General Douglas MacArthur, set out to remove militarism from Japanese life. *Militarism* is the belief that a nation should be ruled by military goals and values.

In late 1945 the Ministry of Education, following occupation orders, stopped budo classes in schools. Occupation officials saw kendo in particular as training for war. In 1946 the Butokukai was dissolved, and many of its leaders were barred from public posts.

Clubs did not vanish overnight. The Kodokan stayed open in Tokyo, and people kept practicing judo privately. Kendo teachers invented a version called *shinai kyōgi*, played in lighter gear with sport-style scoring. It was meant to show kendo as a sport rather than war training.

words.d: the belief that a nation should be run by military goals and values
rule of a country by foreign armies after a war
a sport-style form of kendo created after 1945, with lighter gear and new scoring

check.why: U.S. General Douglas MacArthur led the Allied occupation.

check.why: The Butokukai was dissolved in 1946 under the occupation.

lessons.title: Back as a Sport
lessons.mainIdea: Judo and kendo returned to Japanese schools in the early 1950s as sports run by new national federations.
reading: The All Japan Judo Federation was founded in 1949. It organized judo as a sport with open contests and published rules. In 1950 judo was allowed back into Japanese schools. Officials described it now as physical education and sport.

Kendo took longer because of its link to the sword. The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952, the year the occupation ended. Kendo then returned to school physical education. Its new rules stressed safety, fair scoring and sportsmanship.

The word *federation* matters here. A federation is a group of clubs and regions that agree on rules and hold championships. Budo moved from a state-run society to member *federations* like those in other sports. That change helped judo enter the Olympics in 1964.

words.d: a body made of member clubs or regions that agree on rules and hold championships
fair and respectful conduct toward opponents and officials

lessons.title: Required Again in 2012
lessons.mainIdea: Since 2012 Japanese junior high schools must teach budo, with most choosing judo or kendo, and safety rules followed.
reading: In 2008 Japan's Ministry of Education revised its national *course of study*. The new plan made budo a required part of physical education in the first two years of junior high school. It took full effect in April 2012. Dance became required at the same time.

Schools could choose among judo, kendo and sumo, and some offered other arts. Most chose judo or kendo. The ministry described the goal as learning about Japan's traditional culture and showing respect to others.

Parents and doctors raised concerns about judo injuries among beginners. The ministry and judo bodies responded with *safety guidelines* and teacher training. This return shows a state using budo again, now described as culture and health rather than war.

words.d: Japan's national plan that lists what each school subject must teach
written rules meant to prevent injuries
customs and arts handed down over many generations

lessons.title: Sambo and the Soviet State
lessons.mainIdea: The Soviet Union recognized sambo as an official sport in 1938, building it from judo, local wrestling and military training.
reading: *Sambo* is a Russian short form for self-defense without weapons. It grew in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and 1930s. One of its founders, Vasili Oshchepkov, had studied judo at the Kodokan in Tokyo and earned a black belt there. Another, Viktor Spiridonov, trained police and soldiers.

The Soviet state wanted fit, ready citizens. In 1931 it began a national fitness program called GTO, short for Ready for Labor and Defense. Wrestling styles from many Soviet peoples, such as Georgia and Central Asia, fed into the new sport. So did judo.

In 1938 the All-Union Committee for Physical Culture and Sports recognized sambo as an official sport. The year before, Oshchepkov had been arrested during Stalin's purges, and he died in prison. His story shows that a state could promote an art and still destroy one of its builders.

words.d: a Soviet combat sport whose name means self-defense without weapons; recognized officially in 1938
a government's removal, arrest or killing of people it sees as enemies
Ready for Labor and Defense, a Soviet national fitness program begun in 1931

lessons.title: A Student Writes on Physical Education
lessons.mainIdea: In 1917 a young Mao Zedong argued in a magazine that China's weakness came partly from neglecting physical education.
reading: In April 1917 the Chinese magazine *New Youth* printed an essay called A Study of Physical Education. Its author used a pen name. He was Mao Zedong, then a student at a teachers' school in Changsha, Hunan. He later led the Chinese Communist Party.

Mao wrote that the nation was weak and its people's bodies were weak too. He blamed schools that valued only book learning. He urged daily exercise and called physical education the base of moral and mental growth. The essay reflected a wide belief of the time linking fit bodies to a strong nation.

After the People's Republic was founded in 1949, the state built sport through national committees. A 1950s *slogan* credited to Mao urged people to develop sport and strengthen their health. It was painted on stadium walls. Such slogans tied personal fitness to *national strength*.

words.d: a Chinese magazine of the 1910s that published essays calling for new ideas
a short saying used again and again to spread an idea
the idea that a country's power depends on its people's health and skills

lessons.title: Health Culture or State Project
lessons.mainIdea: Historians ask whether a school martial art served students' health, the state's aims, or both, by reading the stated reasons.
reading: Japan in 1931, the Soviet Union in 1938 and Japan again in 2012 all put combat arts into official programs. Each government gave written reasons. Japan's 1931 plan spoke of loyalty and spirit. The Soviet GTO badge spoke of labor and defense. Japan's 2012 plan spoke of culture and respect.

A *health culture* is a society's shared habits and beliefs about keeping bodies well. A *state project* is a plan a government pushes toward its own goals, such as a stronger army. The same gym class can serve both. Historians look at who wrote the rule, when, and what else the government was doing.

Timing is strong evidence. Japan's required budo came as its army moved into China. Sambo's recognition came during a military buildup. Japan's 2012 rule came in peacetime. Comparing dates with events helps a reader weigh the stated purpose against the likely one.

words.d: a society's shared habits and beliefs about keeping bodies well
a plan a government pushes to reach its own goals
facts or records used to support a claim
